prime.problem: The naive matmul reads its inputs with each warp's 32 loads landing on 32 different rows, getting 15 GB/s from a 768 GB/s card, and every result re-reads 8,184 floats from global memory. Both waste bandwidth in a different way, and fixing one doesn't fix the other.
prime.fits: Second matmul card. It applies the coalescing card to kernel 1's index mapping (kernel 2) and the shared-memory card's tiles to reuse (kernel 3). Kernel 3's profile, MIO throttle, is the problem the blocktiling card solves.
expect: GMEM and SMEM loads per result
prime.goal: Explain why two edited lines give 6.4×, why on-chip tiles give only 1.5× more, and count global and shared loads per result for any block tile.

attend: Kernel 2 changes only which thread computes which entry of C. What does a warp read from A and from B on one step of the loop, before and after?
Why is the SASS identical for kernels 1 and 2 even though one is 6.4× faster?
Kernel 3 cuts global loads 32-fold. Why is it only 1.5× faster?
What does the stall reason "MIO throttle" say is full, and why does that point at shared-memory loads here?
At 66% occupancy with warps often "not selected", why isn't occupancy the problem?

must: Warps are 32 consecutive threadIdx.x → kernel 1 mapped threadIdx.x to rows, so a warp read 32 rows of A 16 KB apart (33 sectors per step) → kernel 2 maps it to columns, so a warp reads 32 neighbouring floats of B plus one broadcast float of A (5 sectors) → GMEM throughput 15 → 110 GB/s, 6.43×
Coalescing fixes bytes per load, not the number of loads → kernel 2 still issues 2K = 8,184 global loads per result (0.25 FLOP/B) → only reuse can cut the count

Load a 32 × 32 tile of A and B into shared memory once per block → each loaded float serves 32 results → GMEM loads per result fall 2K → K/16 (8 FLOP/B) → but every FMA now needs two shared-memory loads (2K per result)

Two LDS per FMA → the MIO queue fills → warps stall on MIO throttle while FMA units idle → the kernel is shared-memory-instruction-bound, not DRAM-bound → the fix is more results per thread (kernel 4)
elevated: Kernel 2 was already getting heavy L1 and broadcast help (≈ 7.95 TB/s of thread-level loads against 110 GB/s measured, ~98.6% served on-chip) → kernel 3 mostly turns implicit cache hits into explicit shared-memory hits → which is why its gain is modest
reference: the ptxas report (37 registers, 8,192 B smem, 400 B cmem)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one warp's reads of A and B for one step of the k-loop in kernel 1 and kernel 2 (sector counts on each). Then write the loads-per-result line for kernels 1, 2 and 3 and circle the number that caused kernel 3's stall.
checklist: kernel 1: 32 rows of A (32 sectors) + one float of B broadcast (1) = 33 sectors
kernel 2: one float of A broadcast (1) + 32 neighbouring floats of B (4) = 5 sectors
kernels 1 and 2: 2K GMEM loads per result; kernel 3: K/16 GMEM, 2K SMEM
2 SMEM loads per FMA fill the MIO queue
coalescing fixes the bytes per load; tiling fixes the number of global loads; neither fixes shared-memory pressure

retrieve.q: Explain why coalescing gave 6.4× but did not change the number of global loads each result needs.
answer: coalescing merges a warp's 32 loads into few sectors, so fewer bytes move per load
each result still reads a full row of A and column of B: 2K loads
cutting the count needs reuse, which is what shared-memory tiles do

retrieve.q: Walk through one iteration of kernel 3's outer loop for one block: who loads what, where the two barriers go, and what each thread computes.
answer: each of 1,024 threads copies one float of A and one of B into As/Bs, coalesced
__syncthreads() so the whole tile is present
each thread does 32 FMAs over its row of As and column of Bs
__syncthreads() again before the next tile overwrites it; then slide along K

retrieve.q: Try a 64 × 64 tile in kernel 3 (one result per thread). What happens to GMEM loads per result, SMEM loads per result, and can you even launch it?
answer: GMEM loads halve: K·(64 + 64)/(64·64) = K/32, 16 FLOP/B
SMEM loads stay 2K per result: still two per FMA, so MIO throttle remains
64 × 64 = 4,096 results at one per thread needs 4,096 threads, over the 1,024-per-block limit: you have to give threads more results anyway

compare.q: Both kernel 3 and the tiled transpose use shared memory after fixing coalescing. Which bottleneck did staging remove in each, and which new one appeared?
answer: transpose: removed wasted DRAM sectors; the new problem was bank conflicts, fixed by padding
kernel 3: removed repeated global loads; the new problem was shared-memory instruction throughput (2 LDS per FMA)
padding can't fix kernel 3, because its loads are conflict-free already; the count is the problem

compare.q: Kernel 3's occupancy calculation (66.7% on the A6000) appears on both cards. Why does this card dismiss occupancy while the occupancy card uses kernel 3 as its worked example, and what would make occupancy the real problem?
answer: the profiler shows warps ready but not selected, so there are enough warps; the limit is the MIO pipe
the occupancy card uses kernel 3 to teach the calculator, not to diagnose it
occupancy would matter if warps stalled on memory latency (long_scoreboard) with few eligible warps

predict.q: Kernel 3's no-cache GMEM ceiling on the H100 is 8 FLOP/B × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TFLOP/s. Commit: if you used a kernel-3-style tiling for a 1,000-token Llama-3.1-8B prefill, about how long would it take compared with the 16.2 ms floor, and which change would you make first?
predict.answer: About 599 ms, 37× the floor: 1.61e13 FLOPs ÷ 26.8e12 FLOP/s. The first change is more results per thread and a larger block tile (kernels 4–5 raise GMEM intensity to 16 and 32 FLOP/B and cut shared-memory loads per FMA), and on an H100 the real answer is tensor-core MMA tiles, because even 32 FLOP/B is far below the 295 ridge.

Then run labs/matmul-ladder.ipynb on a T4 and compute kernel 2 ÷ kernel 1 and kernel 3 ÷ kernel 2.
apply.done: Your table shows K/16 (8 FLOP/B), K/21.3 (10.7) and K/32 (16), with SMEM stuck at 2K in all three and only 32 × 32 launchable, and you have your T4's two step ratios next to the A6000's 6.43× and 1.50×.
apply.hint: GMEM loads per result = K·(BM + BN) ÷ (BM·BN). A 64 × 32 tile at one result per thread needs 2,048 threads.
